entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Avesta is the sacred text of Zoroastrianism, believed to have been composed between the 5th century BCE and the 3rd century CE in ancient Persia, encompassing a vast array of teachings, hymns, and rituals attributed primarily to the prophet Zoroaster. It is significant as the cornerstone of one of the world's oldest monotheistic religions, influencing not only Persian culture but also the broader landscape of religious thought and practice across the globe. The text serves as a reflection of the spiritual, ethical, and social ideals of Zoroastrianism, emphasizing the duality of good and evil and the importance of individual choice in the cosmic struggle between these forces.

The Avesta is comprised of several parts, the most notable being the Yasna, which includes the Gathas—hymns believed to be the direct words of Zoroaster. The compilation reflects the historical context of ancient Persia, showcasing a society grappling with themes of morality, justice, and the divine order. The text was transmitted orally for centuries before being documented, particularly during the Sasanian Empire (224–651 CE), which played a crucial role in preserving Zoroastrian teachings amid the rise of Islam.

In terms of legacy, the Avesta has had a profound impact on later religious traditions, including Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, particularly in concepts of heaven, hell, and the afterlife. The text not only defined Zoroastrian identity but also served as a literary vehicle through which the ethical and philosophical underpinnings of this ancient belief system were passed down through generations. It has been preserved in various forms and continues to be studied and revered by adherents and scholars alike.
